title: Why Ganesha comes first
word: the whole five years in seven sits
hookLine: back at the first doorway: how does anything worth doing begin?
carry: Ganesha is honored before every beginning
tomorrow: after the first words, what did year two open up?
last: LET YOUR TEACHER BE A GOD TO YOU.

cards: A blank document, a cursor blinking at the top of a college essay, and nothing typed yet. The very first word of this path was about exactly that moment. Ganesha, the one at every doorway, honored before anything starts.
Clear the road, then begin. Five years on, standing at the top, the first question comes back around: how does anything worth doing begin?

teach.b: The tradition's answer, from day one: honor the beginning before you begin. Here's why, in the Shiva Purana's telling.
The boy Parvati shaped from earth stood guard at her door and wouldn't let Shiva pass, and in the fight that followed he lost his head. Parvati's grief shook the worlds.

teach.h: AN ELEPHANT'S HEAD, AND A PROMISE.
teach.b: So Shiva brought the boy back with an elephant's head, made him lord of his ganas, and declared he'd be worshipped first, before any other god.
That's why, before a puja, a wedding, a new shop or an exam, Ganesha is honored first, and why some write shri ganeshaya namah at the top of a page. A neighbor tradition also stops at the doorway.
The Qur'an opens with a line known as the bismillah.

teach.h: BISMILLAH: IN THE NAME OF ALLAH.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation: "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful." Muslims say bismillah at beginnings: before a meal, a journey, a piece of work. What's shared is the pause itself.
Before the work, a name is said, and the work is set inside something larger than the worker.
What's honestly different: Hindus honor Ganesha in a form, an image with an elephant's face, often with flowers and a sweet. The bismillah names the one God, Allah, and Islam keeps no images of God.

how: Hindus honor Ganesha first at the start of pujas, weddings, new ventures and studies, often with a short invocation and an offering of flowers or sweets; some write shri ganeshaya namah at the top of a page.

games.q: what does “the whole five years in seven sits” mean?
o: a retreat of silent days spent in a row
a test you must pass to finish the course
a look back over the whole path, from the top

p: honored first, keeper of the threshold
a sweet handed back as a blessing

s: in the Shiva Purana, Shiva declares Ganesha will be worshipped first
after bringing him back with an elephant's head.
every religion begins its work with the same prayer
each has its own words: Ganesha honored first in his form; the bismillah names the one God, with no image.
the Qur'an opens with the words 'In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful'

games.q: your Muslim friend says bismillah before eating; you were raised to honor Ganesha before anything new. what's a fair way to put it?
o: both pause to honor a beginning; she names the one God, you honor Ganesha's form.
they're the same prayer, really, just in two different languages.
hers is a habit, not a prayer, so the two can't be compared.
games.why: a real shared thing, the pause at the doorway, and a real difference in how God is named and imaged. neither has to become the other.

practice: If you can, stand and walk slowly to the nearest doorway. Pause at the threshold and let one breath go all the way out before you step through, then walk back the same slow way.
If you're sitting, take that walk in your mind, and pause at the door just as long.

wordCard.voice: The summit's first look back, to the path's first word: Ganesha, honored first. Clear the road, then begin.

orig.note: Sanskrit: lord of the ganas; the first word of this path, honored at every beginning.

carryVoice: Keep this one: Ganesha is honored before every beginning. It all started at a doorway. See you tomorrow.
